analysis.one_liner: Directs the FCC to build a public AI tool that rates whether communications are likely scams.
analysis.headline: Introduced on November 21, 2024 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Federal Communications Commission to put a free tool on its website within a year. People could submit an email, text message, web link, or a photo of a letter, and an artificial intelligence system would rate how likely it is to be a scam. It is a consumer-protection measure aimed at the flood of phishing texts, robocalls, and mail fraud that costs Americans billions of dollars a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who has received a suspicious text, email, or letter — especially older adults, who are the most common targets of fraud. A free, one-stop tool to check a message before responding could prevent people from sending money or handing over personal information to scammers.

how_it_helps.text: Within one year of enactment, the FCC must offer an online tool that uses artificial intelligence to help the public identify likely scams.
The tool must accept submissions in many forms — emails, text messages, website addresses, and scans or photos of physical mail — and give each one a rating reflecting the likelihood it is a scam.
The bill defines a scam broadly as any scheme to defraud, including communications using false or misleading information to induce someone to pay money or give up personal information.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the development and operation of the tool, and the FCC would take on the technical work of building and maintaining it. No industry pays a direct cost under the bill's text, though senders of mass spam and fraudulent communications lose a countermeasure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers fund the FCC tool

drawbacks.text: An automated rating can be wrong in both directions: it could label a legitimate message as a scam or lend false confidence to a sophisticated fraud the model misses, and people may rely on it instead of their own judgment.
The bill only helps people who check a message before acting; it does not block scam calls, texts, or mail from reaching anyone, so it leaves the underlying problem in place.
It assigns a new technical mandate to the FCC with no dedicated funding provision in the text, leaving the agency to absorb the cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is modest — an FCC website tool paid for out of the federal budget — and the benefit is a free, easy way for ordinary people to check a suspicious message. The main honest objection is that the tool only warns after a scam has already reached someone, and its accuracy would only be as good as the technology. On balance it is a low-cost consumer protection with real but limited reach.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors in the final weeks of the congressional session, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and the session ended before the committee took any action on it.

narrative.text: Representative John Curtis introduced the bill in the House on November 21, 2024.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No other members signed on as cosponsors.
No further action was taken, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the committee or the full House ever considering the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No concentrated interest gained from the bill's death, since it imposed no costs on any industry. The main loss is to consumers, who did not get the fraud-checking tool; the status quo of spam and scam operations continues unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one gained much; status quo continued

for.name: Rep. John R. Curtis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it drew no cosponsors in the remaining weeks of the session.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 21, 2024 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and no votes or recorded opposition show where either party stood.

industries.industry: Mass spam and fraudulent communications operations
industries.note: A widely available scam-rating tool makes it easier for recipients to recognize and reject fraudulent messages, cutting into the effectiveness of phishing texts, robocall fraud, and mail scams. Ordinary people would benefit directly as these schemes get less effective.

The bill does not regulate carriers directly, but a government tool that flags scam calls and texts could add pressure on them to curb the fraudulent traffic that travels over their networks. No direct cost is imposed by the bill's text.
